title: fastjson-c-extension-prototype-for-request-paths-notes
content:
TL;DR:
We prototyped a tiny C-extension (fastjson_mmap) that performs structural JSON scanning + small-object parsing for typical request payloads (~300-4kB). In our microbenchmarks the prototype reduces Python-level parse/tokenize CPU on the hot request path by ~28–45% depending on payload shape, and reduces per-request p99 CPU time for small requests from ~12ms to ~7ms in synthetic single-threaded load. This doc captures assumptions, test harness, specific perf commands and flamegraph pointers, and an experiment plan for a more production-safe iteration.

Background and motivation:
- Problem observed: a sizable fraction of CPU on small requests is spent in Python-level JSON decoding + tokenization and allocation churn when the body is primarily small structured tokens (metadata-only requests, short prompts).
- Existing notes (see linked artifacts) show repeated tail latency spikes where Python frame stacks and PyObject allocations dominate the sampling profiles. Our goal: push inexpensive structural parsing into native code to avoid interpreter overhead for common shapes.

Prototype summary:
- Module: fastjson_mmap (single-source C file, ~460 LOC) exposing two entrypoints: fast_parse_structs(buf) -> list of (offset,length,kind) and fast_extract_small_values(buf, spec) -> bytes for each value per spec.
- Behavior: The module does a single-pass UTF-8-aware structural scan (similar to simdjson's stage 1) but simplified: no full DOM, only returning small-value slices and offsets. For values > 256 bytes or nested arrays we fall back to Python json.loads() on the slice.
- Integration: Hooked into request preproc layer: when Content-Type==application/json and Content-Length < 8k, call fast_parse_structs. If the structure matches a whitelist (top-level obj with string keys that map to string/number/bool/null/plain arrays), map values to Python bytes without heavy allocations and build a light Python dict.

Hypotheses:
1) Most small requests are shallow objects with short strings/numbers; structural scanning in C will cut interpreter overhead by avoiding per-token Python object construction for many fields.
2) The primary win is reduced call-stack depth and fewer PyObject allocations (less time in malloc/jalloc) rather than the raw CPU saved by parsing alone.
3) For non-whitelisted shapes overhead to detect and fallback will cost ~1–2us; acceptable for small fraction of traffic.

Test harness and commands (repro steps):
- Build: gcc -O3 -fPIC -shared -o fastjson_mmap.so fastjson_mmap.c -I/usr/include/python3.10
- Local runner: python -m serving_runtime.bench.fastjson_probe --bind 127.0.0.1:9012 --workers 1
- Load generator: vegeta-like harness in repo: tests/bench/gen_small_requests.py (randomized keys/values seeded for repeatability). Example single-threaded run: 
  for i in 1 2 3; do python tests/bench/bench_runner.py --qps 2000 --duration 60 --body-pattern small_shallow.json --profile py-spy --out run-$i; done
- CPU sampling: sudo perf record -F 250 -g -- python -m serving_runtime.server --config test.yaml ; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded ; flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
- Python sampling: py-spy record -o pyspy.svg -- pid $PID --native --subprocesses --duration 60

Microbenchmark results (single machine, c6i.large-like VM, pinned 2vCPU, no GPU):
- Baseline (no fastjson): single-threaded QPS stable at 2100 req/s, 95th CPU per request ~9.4ms, p99 ~12.1ms. Sampled hot stacks: 38% time in runtime._json.cloads (CPython C impl), 21% in PyUnicode_FromStringAndSize / allocation hotpaths, 12% in Python frame (request preproc).
- Prototype enabled: QPS stable at 2600 req/s, 95th CPU per request ~6.8ms, p99 ~7.2ms. Sampled stacks: 30% time in our fastjson_mmap (C scan), 9% in PyObject allocation paths, 8% in request preproc frames.
- Worst-case (deep/nested payload where fallback used): small regression: ~+1.8ms per-request vs baseline for those inputs (due to detection overhead + double-parse).
- Memory: transient resident set is slightly lower under prototype due to fewer small Python allocations; observed allocation rate measured by tracemalloc decreased ~33% during runs.

Sampling notes and what pointed to C-extension approach:
- py-spy flamegraphs showed repeated short C frames (runtime._json) interleaved with deep Python interpreter frames where GIL was held; many allocations came from PyUnicode_FromKind and list/dict construction.
- perf top with callchains showed the allocator and GC cycle contributions on bursts. Moving structural scan to native code reduced the time spent in allocator hot paths.

Concerns and limitations observed:
- Safety: C buffer slicing requires strict UTF-8 validation; we currently perform an extra validation pass in C which costs ~1% CPU but avoids invalid Unicode errors later.
- Backwards compatibility: some existing code assumes decoded Python strings; switching to bytes for small values required auditing call sites. We added a small wrapper that lazily decodes when a key is accessed as str. That adds complexity and potential memory retention bugs if not careful.
- Fallback correctness: edge cases with escaped unicode and surrogate pairs required robust tests (we added >150 unit tests).

Follow-up experiment ideas (priority ordered):
1) Heap-profiling under high concurrency to understand long-tail allocations per-request with and without prototype (Valgrind/heaptrack run).
2) Run A/B on a subset of traffic in staging with representative workloads (canary 10%): measure real p95 latency and error surface.
3) Try hybrid approach where we only fast-parse a small whitelist of fields (id, prompt_meta, user_id) and leave bulk prompt as string -> safer minimal-surface change.
4) Investigate integrating simdjson (licensed/compat concerns) vs keeping our small focused scanner. Benchmark cost vs benefit.

Open questions for the team:
- How tolerant is product to lazy-decoding bytes->str in middleware? Any customer-facing contract that would break?
- Acceptance policy: what percent of requests are allowed to fall back before we disable this path? Suggest 5% in initial rollout.
- Should we upstream a sanitized version as a shared internal C util (serving-runtime/fastparse) or keep it as isolated prototype until we have 2 quarters of traffic data?

Action items and next steps:
- (Aisha) Clean up the C wrapper, add explicit buffer lifetime docs and remove global static buffers (ETA 2 weeks).
- (Daniel) Coordinate a staging canary (10% traffic) and add metric instrumentation: fastjson_path=true/false, fallback_reasons counter (ETA 1 week).
- (Miguel) Add end-to-end tests for Unicode edgecases and build CI perf job that runs the microbench and fails on regressions >10% (ETA 3 weeks).
- (Priya) Draft product note for engineers describing semantics changes (bytes vs str) and recommended access patterns (ETA 1 week).

Appendix: quick diff of microbench harness (high level):
- bench_runner.py: creates 8 concurrent clients sequentially when --workers 1 to emulate request bursts; records per-request cpu_ns via clock_gettime and emits histogram.
- small_shallow.json: 12 keys, values avg 24 char strings, total ~560 bytes.

Closing thoughts:
This prototype shows clear wins for small, shallow request shapes most common in our hosted API telemetry. The win profile is mostly in allocation reduction and shallower interpreter stacks, not raw parse cycles. If we proceed, we should be conservative in surface area and start with whitelisted fields and a robust canary to watch for functional regressions.

Notes-to-self: keep the prototype isolated under experiments/fastjson_mmap and add a feature-flag gate at the preproc layer.

-- Aisha
